strengths: Novel and well-motivated application of test-time training (TTT) as a streaming long-term memory mechanism for video LLMs, extending prior TTT formulations with a long-span prediction objective that is shown via ablation (Fig. 8, Table 10) to specifically help retention at larger temporal distances between query and evidence.

The proposed ELViM benchmark addresses a genuine and underexplored gap in evaluating episodic/procedural memory in streaming video LLMs (learning from content observed tens of minutes to hours earlier), with a reasonably careful filtering pipeline designed to rule out shortcut answering (Table 6 shows near-chance accuracy without full video and near-ceiling with full video, supporting question validity).

Extensive and informative ablations: comparison of token compression strategies (merging/clustering/discarding), TTTMEM vs Mamba-2 vs vanilla TTT-video, two-stage training contribution, memory-size scaling (Fig. 6), frame-count scaling (Fig. 7), prediction span sweep (Table 10), and deepstack embedding design choice (Table 8) all lend credibility to individual design decisions.

All baselines are reimplemented on the same backbone (Qwen3-VL 8B) and same training data, which is a fair and controlled comparison methodology that isolates the contribution of the memory mechanism itself rather than confounding with backbone/data differences.

Consistent, sizeable improvements are reported across multiple benchmarks (Video-MME, LVBench, VideoEvalPro, ELViM, StreamingBench), and efficiency numbers (Table 3, Appendix D) suggest the added TTTMEM/reading overhead is modest relative to baseline streaming methods, supporting practical deployability claims.
Useful qualitative case studies (Appendix C) illustrating concrete failure modes of non-streaming and PEMF baselines versus the proposed model, adding interpretive value beyond aggregate numbers.
weaknesses: ELViM's question generation, distractor creation, and initial filtering are performed almost entirely by Gemini-2.5-Pro and Qwen3-VL, with only a final 'human collation' step described in one sentence; there is no inter-annotator agreement, no description of annotator qualification, and no analysis of how many questions were rejected/modified during human review, raising concerns about annotation quality and potential model-generation artifacts/biases.

The core technical contribution (TTTMEM) is an incremental extension of existing TTT formulations (Sun et al. 2024; Dalal et al. 2025), primarily adding an auxiliary long-span reconstruction loss; while empirically useful (~1-2% gains in Table 2), the conceptual novelty is limited and the mechanism is not analyzed beyond accuracy deltas (e.g., no analysis of what information the fast weights actually retain).

All experiments use a single backbone (Qwen3-VL 8B); no results are shown with a different LLM backbone or visual encoder to establish that the TTTMEM/reading gains generalize beyond this specific architecture.

No variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the paper, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (e.g., 1-2% differences in some ablation rows) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The claimed '3-hour' streaming capability is demonstrated concretely only via LVBench-style long videos; ELViM's merged videos cap at 90 minutes and average ~49 minutes (Table 4), so the flagship long-duration claim is not directly stress-tested by the newly introduced benchmark.

The modality-aware memory reading mechanism (Section 3.3) is described in dense notation without much intuitive explanation or a simplified pseudo-code walkthrough, hurting reproducibility/accessibility for readers wanting to reimplement it precisely.

Dataset composition for ELViM is restricted to tutorial/how-to YouTube videos in 15 lifestyle categories, which may limit generalizability of memory evaluation to other domains (e.g., narrative video, surveillance, multi-agent interaction) relevant to future agent applications discussed in the introduction/impact statement.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important problem (streaming, long-duration audio-visual understanding under a fixed memory budget) and proposes a reasonably well-motivated extension of TTT (TTT_MEM) with an additional long-span prediction objective intended to combat catastrophic overwriting of fast weights over long sequences.

The empirical comparison is methodologically fairer than much prior work: all baselines (similarity merging, PEMF, non-streaming Qwen3-VL, video-SALMONN 2) are reimplemented on the same backbone and same training data, isolating the effect of the memory mechanism itself.

A reasonably thorough set of ablations is provided (discarding vs merging vs clustering, TTT-video vs Mamba-2 vs TTT_MEM, two-stage training, prediction span T, deepstack embedding handling, memory size and frame-count scaling curves), which helps attribute gains to specific design choices.

The ELViM benchmark targets an interesting and underexplored capability (procedural knowledge retrieval from video observed much earlier combined with real-time task-progress awareness), and the creation pipeline includes a filtering step meant to remove items answerable without watching the full video.
Overhead analysis (TFLOPs, GPU memory, inference latency) shows the proposed mechanism adds negligible runtime cost relative to the backbone, supporting practical deployability claims.
weaknesses: Only a single backbone and model scale (Qwen3-VL 8B) is evaluated; there is no evidence the TTT_MEM mechanism, two-stage training recipe, or reading mechanism generalize to other LLM backbones or larger/smaller model sizes, which is an important gap given the method's claimed generality.

The ELViM benchmark's construction raises circularity/independence concerns: Qwen3-VL (the same model family used as the paper's backbone) is used both to generate/filter questions and as a judge of 'unanswerability,' and Gemini-2.5-Pro is also used for generation. There is no independent human-only verification of filtering outcomes or inter-annotator agreement statistics reported beyond a brief 'manual collate' step, making it harder to rule out benchmark artifacts that happen to favor the proposed architecture.

Hyperparameter selection (e.g., prediction span T in Appendix G, memory-reading chunk sizes) appears to be tuned directly on the same evaluation benchmarks (Video-MME long, LVBench) that are later used to report headline results in Table 1, raising a risk of benchmark overfitting rather than a held-out validation setup.

All reported numbers are single-run point estimates with no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed analysis, making it difficult to assess whether the 1-7% gains on standard long-video benchmarks (smaller than the ELViM gain) are statistically meaningful versus baseline noise.

The audio modality is only superficially integrated: audio tokens bypass TTT_MEM entirely and are merely appended after discarding, so the 'audio-visual' framing and the architectural novelty claimed for multimodal memory are overstated; no audio-specific benchmark or ablation is provided to justify the audio-visual LLM branding.

The core technical novelty is an incremental modification of existing TTT formulations (Sun et al. 2024; Dalal et al. 2025) — adding a long-span reconstruction loss and a discarding-based memory buffer — rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the paper's claim of being 'first' to use TTT for streaming video memory is narrow given closely related prior work (e.g., Wang et al. 2025a on TTT for video, cited but distinguished only by scope of adaptation).

Reproducibility is incomplete in the main text: several architectural/training details (exact gating mechanism, precise learning-rate schedule for fast weights, full LoRA configuration, exact ELViM filtering thresholds) are deferred to citations or omitted, and while code is promised in supplementary material, it is not available for independent verification in this review.

The ablation in Table 2 shows inconsistent trends (e.g., similarity discarding alone is often similar to or worse than similarity merging on some metrics, undermining the paper's stated rationale that discarding is categorically better than merging for TTT_MEM), and the net improvement attributable specifically to the long-span loss versus plain TTT-video is modest (~1 point) and not tested for significance.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated use of test-time training (TTT) as a parametric long-term memory mechanism for streaming video LLMs, going beyond the common token merging/discarding paradigm; the TTTMEM layer's long-span prediction objective is a sensible and empirically justified extension of prior TTT formulations (Sun et al., 2024; Dalal et al., 2025).

Comprehensive ablation studies: comparisons against Mamba-2 and vanilla TTT-video, memory-size scaling curves, frame-count scaling curves, prediction-span sweeps (Table 10), deepstack embedding treatment, and FLOP/runtime overhead analysis (Table 7, Table 3) -- these collectively make a convincing case for each design choice.

The proposed ELViM benchmark addresses a real gap: existing long-video benchmarks mostly test within-clip reasoning or short-term perception, whereas ELViM explicitly probes hours-later recall and procedural knowledge reuse, which is relevant to agentic use cases. The data pipeline includes reasonable leakage controls (post-mid-2025 videos, filtering questions answerable without the full video, human collation).

Strong and consistent empirical gains across multiple long-video benchmarks (Video-MME long, LVBench, VideoEvalPro) and a particularly large improvement on ELViM (up to ~15% absolute), under matched backbone, training data, and memory budget, which strengthens the causal attribution of gains to the memory mechanism rather than confounds.

Practical systems contribution: the modality-aware memory reading mechanism and the two-stage training scheme are shown to meaningfully improve performance while keeping GPU memory and inference time overhead minimal (Table 3), suggesting real deployability under streaming constraints.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single backbone (Qwen3-VL 8B); there is no evidence of generalization to other backbone families or model scales, so it is unclear how much of the method's benefit is backbone-specific versus generally transferable.

ELViM question/timestamp generation and filtering rely on Gemini-2.5-Pro and Qwen3-VL-8B, the same or related model families used elsewhere in the evaluation; this raises a potential circularity/bias concern where benchmark construction artifacts could systematically favor or disfavor certain model behaviors, which is not discussed as a limitation.

Baseline numbers are self-reimplemented versions of prior memory mechanisms (similarity merging, PEMF) rather than the original released systems, and the paper only notes these are "better" than originally reported numbers without fully detailing how implementation choices (e.g., hyperparameters, penalty coefficients for PEMF) were tuned, which could affect the fairness of comparison.

No statistical significance testing, variance across runs, or multiple seeds are reported; given that some gains (e.g., 0.2-0.4% from Stage 2 training) are small, it is hard to assess whether such differences are meaningful or within noise.

Audio tokens bypass the TTTMEM layer entirely and are handled only via the discarding stage, which somewhat undercuts the "audio-visual" framing of the memory mechanism itself; the paper does not evaluate how much audio contributes to the reported long-term memory gains (e.g., on audio-dependent long video QA).

The ELViM benchmark, while valuable, is of modest scale (1849 questions over 1021 target videos) and restricted to tutorial/demonstration video genres, which may limit the diversity of memory-reliance patterns it captures relative to more naturalistic long-form video content.
